detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming societies, economies, and governance worldwide. In the developing era — characterised by rapid digital adoption, economic restructuring, and global interconnectedness — AI promises productivity gains, better public services, and new opportunities. detail.abstract: Analyzing the inclusion of standard terms in the contract for the international sale of goods in electronic form, the author summarizes the existing approaches to this issue and makes the following conclusions. Firstly, the inclusion of standard terms in the contract is regulated by the CISG, but there is no single approach to the procedure of this process. According to one approach, it is enough to simply indicate the intention of one party to include its general terms in the contract. According to another, most common position, it is necessary not only to communicate the intention to include the terms in the contract to the other party, but also to enable the access to the text of the counterparty’s standard terms. More radical approaches require a formal indication in the offer to include standard terms therein, recognizing that simply providing the text of the terms to the other party is insufficient. One way or another, the intention to include the terms in a contract must be clearly expressed, the inclusion must take place either before the conclusion of the main contract, or by reaching a separate agreement between the parties to the existing contract. At the same time, the content of the terms should not be “surprising or unexpected”, otherwise it should be brought to the attention of the acceptor of the general terms. In the case of the “battle of forms”, when both sides offered their standard terms in negotiations, the approach most often used is when the matching terms are considered to be included in the contract (the rest is regulated by the rules applicable by virtue of private international law), but there is also a second approach, according to which those general terms that were sent last and regarding which there were no objections.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the role of emerging technologies in enhancing information interaction within online fashion platforms. Guided by a systematic literature review using the PRISMA framework, four key technologies, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Data-Driven Systems, were examined. Unlike most prior studies that analyzed these technologies in isolation or in limited combinations, this research adopts an integrative perspective. By combining insights from the Dynamic Capabilities View (DCV) (Teece, 1997), the Resource-Based View (RBV) (Barney, 1991), and the Digital Information Interaction Model (Lemon & Verhoef, 2016), it proposes a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes online fashion platforms as information ecosystems rather than mere retail channels. The findings reveal that AI contributes through machine learning algorithms and data personalized information retrieval, AR through digital information layering, VR through the creation of multisensory immersive environments, and Data-Driven Systems through real-time analysis of information flows, each playing a complementary role in strengthening user-data engagement. Importantly, the results highlight the synergistic effects among these technologies: for example, the integration of AI and AR enhances the accuracy of informational outputs, while the combination of VR and Data-Driven Systems enables the design of interactive, data-driven environments. Moreover, the study finds challenges across technical, organizational, ethical, and infrastructural domains, emphasizing the need for algorithmic transparency, ethical data governance, and compliance with regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The proposed framework aids both scholars and practitioners in reframing emerging technologies not merely as marketing tools but as strategic information resources that enhance the quality of information interaction and support sustainable information practices.

detail.title: How Do Commercial Interests and Resource Accessibility Shape Open-Source LLMs: Evidence from Hugging Face
detail.abstract: The emergence of open-source large language models (LLMs) has introduced new challenges to the open-innovation paradigm. Unlike earlier open-source software (OSS), developing LLMs requires substantial computing resources and involves tasks that are not easily divisible. Drawing on data from Hugging Face, we show that open-source LLM development is heavily influenced by commercial interests and disparities in resource accessibility. In particular, improvements in model performance are primarily driven by external contributors affiliated with commercial entities that possess significant computational capacity, and only foundation models released under licenses permitting downstream commercialization benefit from meaningful outside contributions. Interestingly, while OSS contributors can accelerate model adoption, they often channel users disproportionately toward their own derivative models rather than the foundation model, thereby creating a more fragmented ecosystem. This fragmentation—and the resulting erosion of foundation-model market share—is especially pronounced when the OSS contributor has strong commercial interests or access to advanced computing resources. Taken together, these findings highlight a distinct cooperation-competition dynamic between LLM organizations and OSS contributors.

detail.abstract: This article presents the second part of a research project on the tax communications of e-commerce vendors. It details the results of a behavioral experiment designed to test how different representations of sales and use tax obligations influence consumer purchasing decisions. The study finds that potentially misleading indicators, such as "No Tax" or "$0 of Tax," significantly increase the likelihood that consumers will purchase from vendors who do not collect sales tax. detail.title: Moving Markets: Executive Interview Disclosure
detail.abstract: This study investigates the role of CEO interview videos as a form of voluntary information disclosure and their impact on firm market value. While prior research has largely focused on textual and numerical disclosures such as 10-K filings and press releases, the growing use of video-based communication by corporate executives remains understudied. Leveraging a panel dataset of 4,017 firm-year observations from S&P 500 companies between 2010 and 2022, we examine the market effects of CEO interview videos posted on social media platforms, particularly YouTube. Using a staggered difference-indifferences (SDID) approach, we provide causal evidence that video disclosures significantly increase in firm stock prices. Robustness checks using price model, two-stage treatment effects model, placebo tests, and cross-industry analysis confirm the findings. The results show that CEO video disclosures serve as valuable signals to the market. This research extends the literature on information disclosure by incorporating a new media communication channel and highlights the strategic role of executive visibility in shaping investor perception and enhancing firm valuation.

title: 'You Can't Put the Cat Back in the Bag Once It's Out':  Public Understandings, Practices and Imaginaries Concerning Generative AI Among Australians
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW) - Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences and University of New South Wales (UNSW)

detail.title: 'You Can't Put the Cat Back in the Bag Once It's Out':  Public Understandings, Practices and Imaginaries Concerning Generative AI Among Australians
detail.abstract: Since their introduction in late 2022, generative AI applications have proliferated as Big Tech companies seek to encourage widespread adoption from the public. This article reports on the findings from qualitative research conducted in mid-2025 exploring a diverse group of Australian adults' knowledge, everyday practices and imaginaries related to generative AI. Nearly all participants, regardless of their age, gender, ethnicity or geographical location, had experimented with generative AI applications, and many had incorporated them into their quotidian routines. However, far from being enchanted by these technologies, these Australians saw them as little more than mundane software that were now pervasive and therefore unavoidable. Generative AI was described as offering useful tools or helpers for achieving better efficiency, timesaving and productivity in accomplishing routine tasks at home and work. Most participants were aware that the tools frequently generated incorrect information, and therefore required checking, but seemed largely untroubled about this. They expressed concerns about the impacts of possibilities of misinformation, fake information, scams and data privacy issues, and the loss of learning or critical thinking that generative AI use could cause. However, participants also expressed feelings of powerlessness over what they could do to avoid using generative AI in the face of the determination by Big Tech-and in some cases, employers and educational institutions-to promote its use. More profound negative impacts were mostly recounted as abstract or as potential problems in a future world if generative AI development by Big Tech was allowed to progress without government regulation.

detail.title: Scientific Collaborator Recommendation: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: This systematic literature review explores recommender systems designed to facilitate scientific collaboration by identifying effective methodologies, algorithms, and data sources. The review highlights the increasing importance of collaboration in advancing research across disciplines and addresses challenges such as data sparsity, the cold-start problem, and the complexity of modeling interdisciplinary interactions. It examines techniques including machine learning, complex network analysis, and semantic approaches, emphasizing the role of user profiles, research interests, and social influence metrics in improving recommendation relevance and accuracy. The review also discusses strategies to mitigate publication bias, ensure transparency, and enhance the reproducibility of research findings. Additionally, it explores emerging trends like the use of large language models to optimize collaborator suggestions and address the dynamic nature of scientific networks. The study identifies gaps in current approaches, such as handling new researchers and capturing complex collaboration patterns, and suggests future research directions to develop more personalized, scalable, and interdisciplinary recommendation systems. Overall, this review provides a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art in scientific collaborator recommendation systems, aiming to support researchers in forming impactful and diverse collaborations to accelerate scientific discovery.

detail.abstract: Choice modeling is a critical tool for understanding consumer preferences and guiding decisions in fields such as operations management and economics. Traditional choice models typically focus exclusively on consumer decisions, overlooking the fact that, especially in online marketplaces, consumers and sellers mutually select each other. As marketplaces like Airbnb and Upwork grow in economic significance, accurately capturing these mutual choices becomes essential for effective marketplace management. In this study, we propose a two-sided feature-based choice model based on the optimal transport (OT) theory. Our model conceptualizes consumer-seller interactions as two-sided matching, where each pairing generates a surplus that incentivizes both parties to select counterparts maximizing their individual payoffs. To capture inherent randomness in consumer choices, we incorporate a bilinear stochastic surplus function within the OT framework. This formulation effectively models mutual choice behaviors and captures the complexities of contemporary marketplace dynamics. Applying this two-sided choice framework, we address critical marketplace management problems, including platform commission optimization, seller cohort size management and assortment planning, and centralized pricing decisions. Specifically, we establish the unimodality of the revenue function with respect to commission rates that enables efficient commission optimization. For seller cohort management, we demonstrate the concavity of the revenue function in relation to seller cohort sizes, and for seller assortment optimization, we develop a polynomial-time tree-decomposition algorithm. Then, for the centralized price optimization problem, we reveal that optimal centralized prices consistently feature a uniform markup. Furthermore, we provide a nonparametric learning algorithm for model estimation. Numerical results with synthetic and real-world data confirm that the proposed learning algorithm enables more accurate model estimation and yields consistent improvements in commission, assortment, and centralized pricing decisions compared with benchmark methods.

title: China's AI Capitalism: Varieties of Capitalism, State Strategy, and Socio-Cultural Embeddedness in the Pursuit of Technological Dominance

detail.title: China's AI Capitalism: Varieties of Capitalism, State Strategy, and Socio-Cultural Embeddedness in the Pursuit of Technological Dominance

declarations.funderStatement: Erasmus Mundus Consortium

detail.abstract:
Since 1990s, China’s economic growth has been attributed to high government investments, an undervalued currency, inexpensive or cost, and most importantly, the continuation of policies for  longer period (Andreas NOJke, 2020). The 2002 reforms that focused on restructuring organizations for more power consolidation went in Favour of the businesses that had high political linkages. In addition to that, the availability of stimulus packages during crises has made the market a safe breeding ground for large companies as well as start-ups.

 When Jinping took over the leadership of Chinese Communist Party (CCP) 2021, he focused on further refurbishing the economy for ease of business. Although his policies consolidated more control over economic levers for CCP, they created new investment avenues and made the legal system more flexible for technologies (The Economist, 2020). One industry that has significantly flourished under these strategies is the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry. In a time when major economies around the world have started leveraging AI to gain ‘strategic advantage’ over others, China has shown the world the wide range of AI applications and their potential impact on society. Although. initially developed for citizen surveillance and to counter US dominance, by the time other transitional economies joined the AI race, China’s AI was far ahead of others by virtue of its conducive policies and aggressive government investment.

Data privacy and citizen surveillance issues are much neglected in China, hence there is a wide range of AI applications in the public sphere. Currently there are no laws regarding the use of AI, but some guidelines are in place that compels all stakeholders to make data available to the government. The market size, data availability, technological and policy environments of China have helped the industry gain world leadership in technological development and market applications.

 Although the industry has made significant strides in battling COVID-19, it has also been used by the government for controversial purposes namely for the ethnic cleansing of Uighurs, citizen surveillance and military purposes. Furthermore, there have been allegations regarding this growth for lack of core technology development, high dependence on incremental innovation over radical ones and business environment uncertainties.

China’s economic model has been shifting since the 1990s, but only under Xi Jinping’s rule did AI-based companies flourish significantly, both in terms of market expansion and product development. The question arises, what unique characteristics worked in China’s case under Xinomics? What factors impacted this growth? What were the roles of the five pillars as noted by Hall and Soskice and towards which direction? Is this growth reversible or sustainable?

Research of this article was conducted between November to December 2021. The focus area of the study is mainly on mainland China. A qualitative approach was employed in the study, relying primarily on publicly available research, supplemented by data gathered from various international and national institutions, policy documents, conference proceedings, newspaper articles, and journalistic reports.

detail.abstract: On July 30, 2025, President Trump imposed 50% tariffs on imports from Brazil and sanctioned a sitting Brazilian Supreme Court Justice, both partially because of Brazil's online content moderation decisions. This is an extreme, but not an isolated event: worldwide, legislators and regulators struggle to craft public policies that address problems of disinformation and online harassment while protecting the freedom of expression-leading to increasing international confrontations. One key question in content moderation is content adjudication-or who is responsible for deciding what type of speech violates the law and should be taken down. This article presents the results of a six-year, large empirical and qualitative project on the adjudication of fake news disputes by Brazilian Courts from 2018 onwards. It examines what led Brazilian judges to order the takedown of online content, which social networks and types of content were most affected by judicial decisions, and whether there is evidence that incumbent politicians abused the system, among other factors. It also critically analyzes the evolution of this novel court-driven content moderation regime-one in which Courts play an increasingly active role in policing online discourse-with significant implications for the Brazilian information ecosystem, democratic institutions, and judicial reputation. Ultimately, the Brazilian experience teaches/reinforces five lessons to jurisdictions rethinking their online content moderation regulatory regimes: (i) content moderation systems must articulate clear end goals to work properly; (ii) experimentation in content moderation regulation is possible and desirable, allowing for incremental learning and adaptation; (iii) a content moderation system must have strict protection against the slippery slope that may lead it to censorship and arbitrariness; (iv) content-based moderation systems become part of the information environment-claims about neutrality in adjudication cannot, by themselves, support long-term systemic legitimacy; (v) increasing regulatory fragmentation impose new urgency on the development of international guidelines for limits on the extraterritoriality of online decisions.

detail.abstract: The article compares the rhetorical strategies of two of the most popular post-martial law presidents in the Philippines, Joseph Estrada (1998-2001) and Rodrigo Duterte (2016-2022). Adopting Laclau's definition of populism and localizing De Cleen and Stavrakakis's analysis of socio-spatial dichotomies, I examine the political logic that guided the consolidation of the people and the formation of antagonistic frontiers during the Estrada and Duterte presidencies. I identify the nodal points in their articulation of sympathy, compassion, elite opposition, political will, and belongingness, and plot them on a down/up and in/out axes. In uncovering the operation of populist logic in their political speeches, the article finds that leveraging people's frustrations and unsatisfied demands reinforced Estrada's and Duterte's ability to mobilize support and project themselves as the people's protector and champion. Through an in-depth interrogation of their populist articulation, the article contributes to a more nuanced understanding of populism's durability and enduring appeal.

detail.abstract:
Is America still religious? How deeply are our faith communities driven by politics? In an era of deepening polarization, can religious Americans help us transcend politicized narratives and unite around shared values? 

The answers may surprise you. They may even challenge and inspire you to rethink faith in America — and the role that faith communities can play in bringing us together as a country.

Our perception of religion in the United States has become increasingly distorted by partisan politics and misinformed stereotypes. More in Common’s newest report, Promising Revelations, sheds light on false assumptions about faith communities and explores how misperceptions contribute to division in our society. By dispelling common myths about religious America, Promising Revelations paints a hopeful and clear picture of what it means to be a person of faith in America today. 

Drawing on research from more than 6,000 Americans, with a specific focus on Christian, Jewish and Muslim Americans, this study finds significant perception gaps—disparities between what Americans imagine people of faith to believe and what they actually believe. These perception gaps constrain our ability to envision a future where America’s faithful play a central role in helping us navigate division and foster social cohesion.

detail.title: Bellman Operators: Reinforcement Learning, Approximate Dynamic Programming, and Dynamic Programming
detail.abstract: We demonstrate that reinforcement learning (RL), approximate dynamic programming (ADP), and dynamic programming (DP) are unified by the same mathematical framework: Bellman operators and their projected variants. While these research traditions have developed largely in parallel across different communities, they implement variations of the same operator-projection paradigm. We show that algorithms across traditions map directly to each other-TD learning implements stochastic approximation to projected Bellman equations, Q-learning performs sample-based value iteration, and modern deep RL methods are neural implementations of classical ADP techniques. This unification enables cross-fertilization of techniques, provides a common error analysis framework, and offers principled guidelines for algorithm design. We validate this framework with experiments on a GridWorld MDP, empirically demonstrating the performance trade-offs between exact, projected, and sample-based methods.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital ecosystems has elevated the need for robust anomaly detection and data governance frameworks that can safeguard financial systems, strengthen cybersecurity, and foster trust in multicultural societies. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven anomaly detection has emerged as a transformative force in identifying irregularities across domains such as financial regulation, insurance compliance, smart city infrastructures, and data marketplaces. In parallel, the integration of governance principles ensures that AI systems remain transparent, fair, and aligned with ethical and regulatory requirements. This paper investigates how anomaly detection, when embedded in broader governance architectures, enhances resilience in finance, cybersecurity, and smart cities. Special attention is given to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as a global testbed, where tolerance-based governance models intersect with digital transformation, offering lessons for multicultural inclusivity in AI. Drawing on academic and industry sources (Shaffi & Sidhick, 2025; Ratnawat, 2024; Brankovic, 2025), the paper synthesizes case studies from the UAE's financial compliance reforms, Dubai Smart City, Abu Dhabi's digital initiatives, and global regulatory contexts such as LIBOR reform. The findings suggest that anomaly detection, supported by governance structures and multicultural frameworks, can secure digital infrastructures while embedding fairness and trust. The paper concludes by offering a roadmap for policymakers, technologists, and regulators to harmonize AI-driven innovation with inclusive governance in multicultural digital ecosystems.

title: Semantic Physics: Toward a Thermodynamics of Understanding

detail.title: Semantic Physics: Toward a Thermodynamics of Understanding
detail.abstract:
Semantic Physics proposes a new scientific framework that treats meaning not as an abstract construct, but as a measurable physical phenomenon. Current computational systems operate on tokens and correlations, achieving fluency without understanding. This work argues that understanding arises from semantic gradients (∇S) — differences in meaning that generate tension, analogous to thermodynamic or electrical potentials. The flow of meaning is determined by both gradients and structural conductivity (σ), formalized in a constitutive law: B=σ∇S where B denotes semantic flux. 

Building on this foundation, the theory extends to semantic fields: distributed structures characterized by topology, resonance, and stability. Stability is achieved not by static correctness but by resonance — the sustained alignment of gradients and flux — while instability manifests as drift. The Sixth-Order Semantic Operating System (S⁶OS) is introduced as an architecture for regulating these dynamics, and the ΔFold principle as the emergence condition of self-measurement. The implications are broad: from rethinking AI architectures as semantic reactors to framing cultural and scientific attractors as forms of semantic gravitation. Semantic Physics thus marks the transition from token machines to field-based systems — from computation to the thermodynamics of understanding.

detail.title: Is Confidential Supervisory Information Material to Investors? Evaluating the Conflict between Banking and Securities Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: U of Michigan Law & Econ Research Paper No. 25-015
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Michigan Law School, Law & Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: A central goal of modern US securities law is the transparency of corporate information through mandatory public disclosures. This goal is in tension with a central goal of banking law, namely, the practice of preserving opacity of the information exchanged between banks and bank supervisors to ensure the safety and soundness of individual banks and the entire banking system. That informational opacity in banking known as "confidential supervisory information" (CSI) applies equally to all banks, whether or not they sell securities subject to public disclosure requirements. The disclosure of CSI is prohibited by law and practice, with dire consequences for those who violate these prohibitions. How significant is this tension between securities and banking laws? If CSI is always immaterial to investors-the unofficial or de facto position of bank regulators supported by some previous studies of the subject-then the conflict is easy to resolve, but raises questions about what, exactly, the process of bank supervision accomplishes. If some CSI is in fact material to investors, then the failure by companies and insiders to disclose it may violate federal securities law. Using a dataset of unexpected CSI leaks at publicly traded bank holding companies, we empirically assess the materiality of certain CSI to market investors. We find abnormal returns with significant magnitude on days that CSI is unexpectedly leaked. Our findings, therefore, establish that at least some CSI is material to public investors, raising implications for disclosure compliance, insider trading, and regulatory accountability. We also document that unexpected leaks generate significant changes in implied credit default spreads in a direction that is mostly consistent with the documented abnormal returns. The results shed new light on the tradeoffs between opacity and disclosure policies for banking organizations.

detail.title: Determinants of Healthcare Spending in Iranian Households: A Random Forest Approach
detail.abstract: This study employs a Random Forest (RF) model to analyze the determinants of healthcare expenditure ratios (HER) among Iranian households, using data from the 2022 Iranian Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HEIS). The research addresses critical gaps in understanding how socioeconomic, demographic, and geographic factors interact to shape healthcare spending patterns in Iran, particularly in the context of post-Health Transformation Plan (HTP) reforms. Key findings reveal that: Regional disparities (province of residence) are the strongest predictor of HER (%IncMSE: 62.38%), with rural households allocating 6% of their total expenditures to healthcare compared to 5% in urban areas. Income inequality significantly influences HER, as households in the lowest income quartile spend 10% of their budget on healthcare, versus 2% in the highest quartile, highlighting vulnerabilities to catastrophic health expenditures (CHE). Education exhibits a dual role: higher literacy correlates with preventive care utilization but also increases demand for specialized services, elevating costs. Elderly-heavy households and those with unstable employment face disproportionately higher healthcare burdens. Methodologically, the RF model outperforms traditional linear approaches by capturing non-linear interactions among variables, achieving an R² of 0.0598 and RMSE of 0.0849. The study underscores the need for targeted policy interventions, including: Geographically tailored insurance schemes for highrisk provinces (e.g., Sistan-Baluchestan). Progressive subsidies to mitigate financial strain on lowincome and rural households. Expansion of preventive care infrastructure to reduce long-term costs. By integrating machine learning with health economics, this research provides actionable insights for advancing equitable healthcare financing and achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) in Iran.

title: From Digital Disadvantage to Strategic Asset: Tacit Knowledge of the Digital Divide Generation in the GenAI Era

detail.title: From Digital Disadvantage to Strategic Asset: Tacit Knowledge of the Digital Divide Generation in the GenAI Era
detail.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly standardizing and commodifying explicit, codified knowledge. While GenAI excels in processing and reproducing digitalized information, it struggles with tacit, experiential knowledge that remains embedded in individuals and generations. This conceptual paper reconceptualizes the "digital divide generation"-adults who faced high adaptation costs during the digital transition-as a strategic source of tacit knowledge in the GenAI era. Drawing on Nonaka's tacit-explicit distinction, Becker's human capital theory, and Barney's resource-based view, we argue that the GenAI-driven equalization of explicit knowledge raises the relative value of tacit expertise. We propose a 2×2 framework (knowledge type × GenAI role: substitute vs. complement) and highlight how organizational advantage emerges in the "tacit × GenAI-complement" quadrant, where human judgment, relational coordination, and shop-floor know-how combine with GenAI's data-processing capabilities. By framing tacit knowledge as a modern form of intangible cultural heritage, the paper specifies conditions, mechanisms, and boundary factors that determine its value and transfer. This perspective advances a human-AI complementarity view of knowledge management and innovation, and offers implications for intergenerational knowledge transfer, organizational practice, and policy design.

title: Inequality of Opportunity in an Urban Context: Evidence from Mexico City Using Machine Learning and Roemer's Framework

detail.title: Inequality of Opportunity in an Urban Context: Evidence from Mexico City Using Machine Learning and Roemer's Framework
detail.abstract: This study applies the rigorous methodological framework of Brunori, Hufe, and Mahler (2018) operationalizing John Roemer's theory of equality of opportunity-to quantify and analyze Inequality of Opportunity (IOp) in Mexico City. Using data from the 2010 Mexican National Census, we construct a wealth index via factor analysis and employ conditional inference trees to algorithmically identify circumstance-based types, avoiding arbitrary categorizations. Type-specific wealth distributions are smoothed using Bernstein polynomials to define Roemerian effort tranches. We compute both ex-ante (between-types) and ex-post (within-tranches) IOp measures. Our results indicate that Mexico City exhibits a relatively low level of IOp compared to national averages, with an ex-post Gini of 0.0837, meaning circumstances account for 48.85% of total inequality. However, the opportunity structure is highly concentrated, dominated by just three social types that explain 100% of the model's variation. This paradox reveals a context where individual effort is significant (explaining 90.19% of between-tranche inequality), yet initial circumstances create a stark hierarchy of advantage and significantly bias outcomes even for individuals exerting similar effort. The study confirms the findings of Plassot et al. (2021) at the national level while providing a more granular and contrasting view of the opportunity structure within the capital, highlighting the critical influence of unobserved parental wealth and pointing to profound territorial segregation within the city.

detail.abstract: How do the idiosyncratic responses of the households influence the transmission of monetary policy into the granular level consumption expenditure in India? This study applies an approach of Local Projection Instrumental Variable (LP-IV) regression to estimate the Dynamic Causal Effects of a 25-bps contractionary monetary policy shock on household-level consumption expenditures. Impulse Responses of a conventional contractionary monetary shock show a persistent but lagged negative effect on household expenditure, following a positive effect on consumption expenditure in the immediate horizons. Rural households show more sensitivity to the positive impulse compared to their urban counterparts. Two layers of middle-income households capture a greater response to the shock across the regions. We also show an empirical decomposition of the direct and indirect effects of the monetary policy shock on household consumption. We argue for a Sticky Debt that makes household consumption expenditure of rural and middle-income groups different from others to corroborate our findings.

title: When Saving Meets Investment: How Shocks Shape the Feldstein-Horioka Puzzle

detail.title: When Saving Meets Investment: How Shocks Shape the Feldstein-Horioka Puzzle

declarations.funderStatement: This research was financially supported by the subsidy granted to the Krakow University of Economics (grant no. 021/EEM/2023/POT) and by the Polish Minister of Science and Higher Education under the ”Regional Initiative of Excellence” programme.

detail.abstract: This paper offers a new perspective on the Feldstein-Horioka puzzle by highlighting the central role of macroeconomic shocks in shaping the time-series correlation between investment and saving-captured by the saving-retention coefficient-in advanced and emerging market economies. We argue that the coefficient reflects the relative importance of shocks and responses of investment and saving to them rather than the level of international capital mobility. To build intuition, we first demonstrate how different shocks shift the distribution of the saving-retention and then link the coefficient analytically to shock characteristics in linear dynamic macroeconomic models. Using estimated open-economy DSGE models for nearly 60 countries over the past 50-60 years, we document substantial country-level heterogeneity in the saving-retention coefficients and relate it to the incidence and magnitude of shocks, as well as the different responses of investment and saving to shocks. Specifically, domestic demand shocks, like preference and public spending shocks, tend to raise the saving-retention coefficient due to their similar effects on investment and saving. In contrast, foreign shocks, such as global interest rate and risk premium disturbances, typically reduce the coefficient but contribute little to fluctuations in saving. Furthermore, the dissimilar responses of investment and saving to technology shocks, especially permanent ones, emerge as the primary source of the higher coefficient values observed in advanced economies compared to emerging markets. Overall, our findings challenge conventional interpretations of the Feldstein-Horioka puzzle and underscore the dominant role macroeconomic shocks play in shaping investment-saving dynamics over time.

detail.title: Medication-Based Mortality Prediction in COPD Using Machine Learning and Conventional Statistical Methods
detail.abstract: Background: Predicting mortality in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients supports clinical decision-making and resource allocation. While most existing prediction models rely on clinical, physiological, imaging, or biological measures which are not frequently collected in clinical practice, drug claims data may be electronically accessible during routine visits.Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of COPD patients aged ≥40 years in Quebec with ≥2 years of public drug coverage and ≥1 dispensation of maintenance COPD medication. Predictors included sociodemographic characteristics, medication use and adherence for COPD and, in some models, for other chronic conditions. We compared logistic regression to six machine learning (ML) methods and assessed their performance in predicting 5-year all-cause mortality on a separate test set.Results: Among 179,168 COPD patients (mean age 70.2 years; 47.4% male), five-year mortality rate was 24.3%. Logistic regression achieved an area under the receiver-operator characteristics curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.7485 using only COPD medications, rising to 0.7784 when adding medications for other chronic diseases. Most ML methods slightly outperformed logistic regression, with deep artificial neural networks (D-ANN) yielding the best performance (AUC-ROC = 0.7870; p < 0.001). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis highlighted non-inhaled anticholinergics, diuretics, antidepressants, and lipid-lowering agents as top predictors.Conclusions: Models using medication-based predictors can effectively estimate five-year all-cause mortality in COPD patients. Including medications for other chronic diseases improved model performance. While ML approaches, especially D-ANN, showed improved performance, gains over logistic regression were modest. Models based on drug claims are alternatives for risk stratification during routine visits.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in organizations. We ask: (1) How should a principal optimally deploy limited AI resources to replace workers in a team? (2) In a sequential workflow, which workers face the highest risk of AI replacement? (3) How does substitution with AI affect both the replaced and non-replaced workers’ wages? We develop a sequential team production model in which a principal can use peer monitoring—where each worker observes the effort of their predecessor—to discipline team members. The principal may replace some workers with AI agents, whose actions are not subject to moral hazard. Our analysis yields four key results. First, the optimal AI strategy stochastically replaces workers rather than fixating on a single position. Second, the principal replaces workers at the beginning and at the end of the workflow, but does not replace the middle worker, since this worker is crucial for sustaining the flow of information obtained by peer monitoring. Third, the principal may optimally underutilize available AI capacity. Fourth, the optimal AI adoption increases average wages and reduces intra-team wage inequality.

detail.abstract: Regulatory intervention is important in shaping corporate behaviour, especially in markets with relatively weak property rights. Using a sample of publicly listed companies in China from 2006 to 2021, this study investigates the impact of regulatory intervention on managers' misconduct and corporate idiosyncratic risk. Using a difference-indifferences design, we compare the idiosyncratic risk after inspections of a manager's misconduct to that of their counterparts who are not involved in misconduct activities. We find that inspections of corporate managers' misconduct significantly reduce their firms' risk by weakening investors' heterogeneous beliefs and improving corporate transparency. This effect is more pronounced in firms with lower levels of information transparency and greater external attention pressure, suggesting that regulatory interventions in managers' misconduct could improve corporate information environment.

detail.abstract:
Inflation surged in 2021-2023 from a classic fiscal shock: money and debt that financed huge spending, without a plan for repayment. Neither money nor supply shocks offer a coherent alternative explanation. Inflation eased, with no recession, once the fiscal shock was over. Higher interest rates could have brought inflation down earlier, but could not have stopped it. Going forward, higher interest rates will raise debt service costs, and thus perversely raise inflation unless fiscal policy can tighten. High debt and structural deficits also mean that the US may lose the fiscal space to borrow in the next crisis.

detail.abstract:
Fine-grained migration data illuminate important demographic, environmental, and health phenomena. However, migration datasets within the United States remain lacking: publicly available Census data are neither spatially nor temporally granular, and proprietary data have higher resolution but demographic and other biases. To address these limitations, we develop a scalable iterative-proportional-fitting based method that reconciles high-resolution but biased proprietary data with low-resolution but more reliable Census data. We apply this method to produce MIGRATE, a dataset of annual migration matrices from 2010-2019 that captures flows between 47.4 billion pairs of Census Block Groups — about four thousand times more granular than publicly available data. These estimates are highly correlated with external ground-truth datasets, and improve accuracy and reduce bias relative to raw proprietary data. We use MIGRATE to analyze both national and local migration patterns. Nationally, we document temporal and demographic variation in homophily, upward mobility, and moving distance: for example, we find that people are increasingly likely to move to top-income-quartile CBGs and identify racial disparities in upward mobility. We also show that MIGRATE can illuminate important local migration patterns, including out-migration in response to California wildfires, that are invisible in coarser previous datasets. We publicly release MIGRATE to provide a resource for migration research in the social, environmental, and health sciences.

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper studies how colonial religious institutions reshaped traditional social structures in Africa. Focusing on the Congo, I examine the long-term effects of Christian missions that sought to replace kin-based authority with European-Christian notions of social and moral order. I combine newly digitized data on historical mission locations with an original survey of 975 respondents, measuring attitudes toward family and coethnics, social network composition, referral behavior in a job experiment, and moral values. To address concerns about endogenous mission placement, I construct two counterfactuals: missions that were initially established but later abandoned, and simulated locations that were historically suitable but never selected. I find that exposure to missions persistently reduced bias toward kin and coethnics and weakened the role of kinship ties in networks and referrals. It also eroded communal moral values, such as loyalty to one's group and deference to authority, without a corresponding rise in universal moral principles. Instead, these shifts reflect a redirection of identity and moral obligation from kinship and ethnicity toward religious affiliation. Historical records on mission personnel and infrastructure point to religious instruction and education as key transmission channels. Together, the findings suggest that colonial religious institutions profoundly reshaped the social and moral organization of colonized societies.

detail.abstract: Social interactions between young and senior colleagues might have consequences for union membership uptake of young workers, thus influencing public policies on unions. We apply Norwegian administrative register data to test this claim about the influence of social interactions on unionization, while addressing threats of homophily bias, contextual, and network confounding. Leveraging exogenous spillover shocks by colleagues’ siblings’ unionization to colleagues’ unionization, we find causal evidence supporting the notion that social interactions with close colleagues are important for unionization, mainly driven by social costs and information sharing. Our results suggest that one standard deviation increase in the union density of close colleagues, causes the uptake of union membership for young workers to grow by 20-23 percent. Our analyses thus reveal one source of additional spillover impacts from the implementation of public policies supporting unions. Furthermore, our results have important implications for unions’ mobilization strategies.

detail.title: Access for Appraisal: A Review and Framework for Estimating Transport Benefits via Real-Estate Uplift
detail.abstract: This paper reviews real-estate uplift in transport appraisal, synthesising evidence and practice, and proposes a framework for implementation. The literature on real-estate capitalisation in response to transport investments is large, but shrinks considerably when limited to applications in economic appraisal. Across the fourteen studies identified, methods are heterogeneous and theory is thin. Ex-post evaluations mostly use Difference-in-Differences (DID) with distance-based benefit measures and offer little guidance for ex-ante appraisal; ex-ante studies rely on cross-sectional models with limited causal identification and little separation of bidding and sorting. Appraisal is typically demonstrative, aggregating property value changes while neglecting externalities, supply responses, and hedonic assumptions; many report uplift exceeding direct user benefits. We next synthesise a real-estate-based appraisal framework comprising fixed supply, market clearing, and market failure, chosen by project scale, land-use change, and empirical narrative. We highlight issues in benefit incidence and agglomeration double counting. Priorities for further research include DID event studies applied to ex-ante appraisal, modelling floor space supply in hedonics, and establishing agglomeration elasticities through the real-estate market.

detail.title: Volatility Forecasting Factors
detail.abstract: This paper examines the predictive role of high-frequency factor volatilities in modeling the volatility of individual stocks. We develop a dynamic forecasting framework that selects the most informative factor-specific realized volatility from a large cross-section of asset pricing anomalies. Embedded in a log-linear specification, the model integrates both market-wide and idiosyncratic components, allowing for a flexible representation of volatility dynamics. We prove the strong consistency of our selection procedure, and show that our selection rule asymptotically identifies the factor that truly drives volatility. We further show how measurement errors affect the adaptive selection. Empirical results based on a broad universe of U.S. equities demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms standard benchmarks, both statistically and economically. The findings underscore the importance of incorporating high-frequency cross-sectional information in volatility modeling, offering a scalable and interpretable approach to understanding time-varying risks in equity markets.

Off-Balance-Sheet Fiscal Agencies in Wars, Reconstruction, and the Green Transition” (OBFA-TRANSFORM) carried out at Global Climate Forum and Freie Universität Berlin (project number 499921148). Details about the research group can be retrieved at https://obfa-transform.eu.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the British state mobilises off-balance-sheet fiscal agencies to address extreme financial pressures inflicted by systemic shocks. It looks at the case of the UK’s Exchange Equalisation Account (EEA), a World War Two (WWII) Treasury-controlled fund operated via the Bank of England, initially established to smooth out exchange rate fluctuations through secret foreign exchange and gold transactions after the pound was taken off the Gold Standard and allowed to float. This experience gained in exchange rate management gave the British authorities a powerful macroeconomic tool, severely lacking in the early interwar period. With the onset of WWII, the EEA’s mandate expanded dramatically: it absorbed the nation's gold reserves, commandeered foreign securities, and underpinned Britain’s issuance of sterling-denominated liabilities to finance wartime imports and expenditures, all the while keeping these activities outside the official government balance sheet. Drawing on extensive archival sources and time-series data, the paper scrutinises the EEA through the lens of the Monetary Architecture framework, which gauges the international monetary and financial system as a hierarchical web of interlocking balance sheets shaped by political and institutional power, through which liquidity and credit are distributed and contested. From this perspective, the EEA operated as a critical sovereign liquidity facility, enabling Britain to fund large-scale war mobilisation without overtly breaching norms of fiscal orthodoxy or destabilising sterling’s international position. In doing so, it exemplifies how states deploy hidden financial infrastructures to manage monetary-fiscal boundaries and navigate systemic shocks.

title: Plugging the Leaks: Reassessing the UK General Anti-Abuse Rule in Light of Practical and Doctrinal Failures

detail.title: Plugging the Leaks: Reassessing the UK General Anti-Abuse Rule in Light of Practical and Doctrinal Failures
detail.abstract: This paper offers a doctrinal and policy reassessment of the United Kingdom’s General Anti-Abuse Rule (GAAR), introduced by Schedule 43 to the Finance Act 2013. Conceived as a principled legislative safeguard against abusive tax avoidance, GAAR has failed to deliver either certainty or deterrence. Its central test—the “double reasonableness” standard—is circular and legally indeterminate. Its institutional machinery—the GAAR Advisory Panel—produces non-binding opinions insulated from judicial scrutiny. Its enforcement record is minimal, opaque, and doctrinally unproductive. Moreover, GAAR’s relationship with adjacent regimes—DOTAS, TAARs, and OECD BEPS measures—remains undefined, creating duplication and systemic incoherence. Through comparative analysis with Australia and Canada, where general anti-avoidance rules have generated more structured jurisprudence, the paper argues that the UK GAAR suffers from design flaws that undermine constitutional principles of legality, certainty, and proportionality. It proposes statutory reform to replace the double reasonableness test with structured indicia of abuse, to transform the Advisory Panel into an adjudicative body, to impose transparency obligations on HMRC, and to integrate GAAR coherently with specific anti-avoidance regimes. The argument is that GAAR should not be abandoned but rebuilt: reconstituted into a credible, principled, and proportionate safeguard that restores coherence to the UK’s anti-avoidance framework.

Bangladesh's urban population in 2023 will rise to 40.47%, and it is expected that projected demographic models predict this figure to increase to 56% by the year 2050, therefore, effectively functioning local governance is an imperative for attaining Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and tackling the complex manifestations of poverty, vulnerability and social exclusion that are essentially localized. title: The Universal Lexicon: Generative AI Chatbots and Fair Use of Works in a Training Corpus
affiliations: Florida International University College of Law

detail.title: The Universal Lexicon: Generative AI Chatbots and Fair Use of Works in a Training Corpus

publicationDetails.detailsText: Florida International University Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Florida International University College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
For centuries, research publications, encyclopedias, and lexicons have helped advance knowledge by drawing freely on expressive works, without seeking licenses for most of what they reference or “use.” Today, that longstanding practice is under new and intense scrutiny.  One pressing question is whether chatbots powered artificial intelligence (AI) should be treated differently.  Major copyright holders, including The New York Times, leading authors, and powerful music rights organizations, have filed lawsuits against companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.  They argue that the training and output of AI systems infringe the exclusive rights of copyright holders, principally the rights of reproduction, distribution, and preparation of derivative works.  The Supreme Court’s decision in Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts v. Goldsmith has raised the stakes in this copyright controversy by narrowing the meaning of transformative fair use and casting fresh doubt on whether copyright law still permits the creation of generative AI (gen-AI) models as modern lexicons of knowledge.

This article examines prior copyright claims against lexicons, scholarly works, and directories, among other technologies and creations, and explains why the right to release a universal lexicon of culture and thought must be defended.  At stake is not simply a technical question of doctrine, but the future of tools that help society organize and expand human knowledge.  First, the purpose of a lexicon or grand encyclopedia differs fundamentally from that of novels, songs, or other creative works, or even individual news articles, press releases, or webpages.  Courts have long recognized that reference works, like news reporting and scholarship, serve purposes that fair use protects, precisely because they promote the progress of knowledge rather than mere entertainment.  Second, the amount and substantiality of what is used in AI outputs can often be negligible.  Any fragment that may appear in output is generally tiny, both in absolute terms and as a proportion of the original work, and rarely, if ever, recreates the expressive heart of that work.  Third, efforts to prohibit research-based creativity by invoking hypothetical licensing markets threaten to dismantle fair use itself.  They invite a circular reasoning process in which any unpaid use is treated as illegal harm simply because it could have been licensed.  Some courts have rightly rejected this logic and have insisted that fair use requires rightsholders to demonstrate a real and direct connection between a specific use and actual loss, whether in sales, profits, or other market value. Mere claims that a license might have been sold are not enough.  What follows is an analysis of why generative AI models fit within the longstanding protections of fair use, and how courts should apply similarity-related principles of fact, genre, and research to defend the creation of these modern lexicons.

title: Role of temporal variation of spatial inequality in epidemiology

detail.title: Role of temporal variation of spatial inequality in epidemiology
detail.abstract: Infectious diseases change epicenters with time. This leads to a temporal variation of spatial inequality in the region-wise number of infected and dead people. We can obtain many important facts related to infectious disease simply by studying the pattern of temporal variation. This is the main purpose of the present study. As this requires, plenty of data over a considerable time span, here we have considered the state-wise number of infected and dead people due to COVID-19 to study temporal variation spatial inequalities. In India COVID-19 started to spread around March, 2020 and reached final endemic equilibrium around July 2022. So, we have considered this duration of time to study how spatial inequality in state-wise number of infected and dead people evolved. This study hints the possible realistic maxima of inequality in case of an unrestricted social issue like a new type of infectious disease like COVID-19. Here we have also found that temporal variation of spatial inequality helps to predict when overall infection rate or death rate of a country will rise or fall. It also indicates how the equality indexes under study are interrelated with each other. We have also compared the outcomes of these study with other social issues like inequality in citation of published paper by various Nobel laureates of different fields and found that the outcomes are similar. This further enhances the importance of the outcomes of the study.

title: An Honest Assessment of Realized Volatility Forecasting with Feed-Forward Neural Networks and Traditional Models: Evidence from International Equity Markets under Normal Conditions and the COVID-19 Crisis

detail.title: An Honest Assessment of Realized Volatility Forecasting with Feed-Forward Neural Networks and Traditional Models: Evidence from International Equity Markets under Normal Conditions and the COVID-19 Crisis
detail.abstract: This thesis provides a comprehensive evaluation of machine learning models versus traditional econometric approaches for realized volatility forecasting using high-frequency data from eight major stock indices (AEX, FTSE 100, S&P 500, Dow Jones, DAX, CAC 40, FTSE MIB, IBEX 35) spanning 2000-2021. Four feed-forward neural networks of varying architectures are compared against the HAR-RV model (Corsi, 2009) and GARCH(1,1), with their performance evaluated under three loss functions: MSE, MAE, and QLIKE. The analysis yields three key findings. First, the parsimonious HAR-RV model demonstrates unambiguous superiority across all evaluation metrics, significantly outperforming both the best-performing FFNN architecture (16 × 8 × 4) and GARCH(1,1). Second, FFNN performance exhibits a nonmonotonic relationship with architectural complexity. The moderate-depth network (16×8×4) approaches but never surpasses HAR-RV's performance, while deeper architectures show diminishing returns. Third, model rankings remain remarkably stable during the COVID-19 crisis. HAR-RV maintains its dominance and demonstrates superior crisis robustness. These findings contrast with recent literature, particularly Christensen et al. (2023). It is concluded that the reported advantages of FFNNs in volatility forecasting are contingent on specific implementation choices, including feature engineering, ensemble methods, regularization techniques, and market regimes.

title: Strategic vs Financial Buyers in AI M&A : A Behavioural and Valuation Comparison
affiliations: Arkstons Investments Limited, affiliation not provided to SSRN, , , , St Anne's College, the University of Oxford and

detail.title: Strategic vs Financial Buyers in AI M&A : A Behavioural and Valuation Comparison
detail.abstract:
This white paper examines how strategic and financial buyers approach artificial intelligence (AI) mergers and acquisitions (M&A), highlighting the behavioural, valuation, and outcome differences between the two. Strategics pay higher revenue multiples for distribution and moat fit; financial sponsors pay for clean unit economics and near-term cash generation; process design can swing outcomes.
The rise in AI-related M&A has reshaped technology dealmaking, with both corporate and private equity firms aggressively pursuing AI assets to capture value from the rapid adoption of machine learning, data infrastructure, and automation. Global AI transactions have accelerated since 2018, reflecting both strategic imperatives and financial opportunities.
As AI deal activity has surged, the motivations and methods of acquirers diverge sharply. Strategic buyers seek acquisitions to deepen their ecosystems, secure proprietary datasets, and gain scarce AI talent, while financial buyers concentrate on operational scalability, recurring revenues, and disciplined exit planning.
This paper provides an evidence-based comparison of buyer behaviour, valuation multiples, and post-deal trajectories. By analysing 30–50 AI-focused transactions between 2018 and 2024, the paper show that strategic buyers frequently pay significant premiums and justify them through synergies, integration, and competitive defence. Financial buyers, in contrast, deploy leverage to target cash-generative SaaS and cybersecurity firms, achieving mid-term returns with less emphasis on innovation continuity.
For founders, investors, and advisors, these insights clarify the trade-offs inherent in different buyer types and provide a practical framework for evaluating AI M&A. Strategic acquirers may accelerate growth and provide premium valuations but reduce independence, while financial buyers often preserve management continuity and offer structured liquidity at the cost of lower upfront multiples.

detail.abstract:
The report, building upon the HKIMR's prior research on demographic changes and long-term asset markets, provides a comprehensive and updated analysis of Hong Kong's long-term investing landscape and opportunities within the context of an evolving digital economy. The report covers two surveys that were commissioned by the HKIMR. The first survey, carried out in collaboration with the Investor and Financial Education Council, explored Hong Kong residents' long-term investment decisions. The second survey, administered in collaboration with a consulting firm, focused on local market participants to gain insight into their perspectives on product development, distribution strategies, and the adoption of technology. 

The study highlights that while Hong Kong residents exhibit a strong foundation for basic financial knowledge, there is a need for greater awareness of specific financial products, particularly those related to long-term investing and financial planning. As for products, Hong Kong already possesses a diverse suite of globally competitive accumulation products. However, 67 per cent of the surveyed market participants saw the crucial need to increase the supply of decumulation product options to accommodate their customers' demand for long-term financial planning.
      
The study also reflects that digital adoption among both survey groups is high. In the study, 72 per cent of surveyed residents reported using digital financial services in the past year, and about 70 per cent of the surveyed market participants reported they are currently adopting or plan to adopt mobile and web platforms to distribute long-term financial products. Based on these survey findings, the study suggests some considerations to foster a healthy long-term investment ecosystem in Hong Kong. Among those, embracing frontier technologies is key to drive innovative product and services, increase cost efficiency, and further enhance product distribution to support more effective long-term investing and financial planning.

title: Cultivating Sustainable Future: The Empowering Journey of the Farmers' Cooperative of Sikkim in Organic Transformation
affiliations: University of Agriculture Faisalabad

detail.title: Cultivating Sustainable Future: The Empowering Journey of the Farmers' Cooperative of Sikkim in Organic Transformation
detail.abstract: The Farmers' Cooperative of Sikkim represents a groundbreaking paradigm in sustainable agriculture, transforming the small northeastern Indian state into India's first fully organic state by 2016. Established in 1995, this cooperative has grown to encompass nearly 60,000 smallholder farmers, with over 90% certified as organic producers, cultivating a diverse array of more than 70 organic crops. This comprehensive study delves into the cooperative's profound impact across economic, social, and environmental dimensions. Economically, it has achieved remarkable success, with earnings exceeding ₹500 crore by 2022, leading to a 30% average income increase for members and improved access to healthcare and education. Socially, the cooperative has empowered over 40,000 farmers through extensive training programs focused on sustainable practices, organic pest control, soil health, and crop rotation, fostering a strong sense of community and collaboration. Environmentally, it promotes biodiversity and ecosystem health through eco-friendly methods such as integrated pest management and agroforestry, enhancing soil fertility and reducing degradation. Despite these achievements, the cooperative faces significant challenges, including market fluctuations-such as a 20% decline in cardamom prices in 2023 due to oversupply-climate change impacts like a 25% increase in rainfall uncertainty and a 1.5°C temperature rise over the past decade, inadequate infrastructure with only 30% of communities having proper road access, limited financial services, and emerging pest management issues following the shift to organic farming. To address these, the cooperative has implemented strategic initiatives: market stabilization through longterm vendor agreements and direct marketing, which has boosted farmer revenue by 15%; climate resilience via agroforestry and crop diversification, improving yields by up to 20%; infrastructure development through collaborations with government and NGOs, aiming to increase market access by 40% in five years; pest control training with agricultural colleges; and financial support via microfinance partnerships to enhance access to organic inputs. Looking ahead, the cooperative is well-positioned for future growth, leveraging export opportunities in the global organic food market projected to reach $320 billion by 2025, with Sikkim's cardamom and ginger gaining traction internationally. Additionally, the integration of ecotourism capitalizes on the state's unique agricultural topography, offering hands-on experiences that boost farmer income while raising awareness of sustainable practices. Digital transformation through ecommerce platforms enhances direct sales, amplifying market reach and customer engagement. Ongoing research partnerships aim to develop innovative solutions for climate adaptation and pest control. This study concludes that the Farmers' Cooperative of Sikkim serves as an inspiring model for policymakers, agriculturalists, and communities worldwide, demonstrating how collective action can revolutionize agriculture, enhance farmer welfare, and promote environmental sustainability. The lessons from Sikkim's journey hold the potential to inspire similar initiatives across Asia and beyond, fostering a resilient and sustainable food system.

title: Consumption Income Analysis -Rural-Urban Disparities Across Six Districts in Maharashtra, India
affiliations: Ramniranjan Jhunjhunwala (Autonomous) College and K.J.Somaiya Institute of Management Studies

detail.title: Consumption Income Analysis -Rural-Urban Disparities Across Six Districts in Maharashtra, India
detail.abstract: This study takes a closer look at how household spending habits in Maharashtra have changed before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. It zeroes in on six key districts-Mumbai, Pune, Nashik, Nagpur, Aurangabad, and Amravati-and examines spending across three vital categories: food, health, and leisure (which includes recreation, dining out, and vacations). By analyzing secondary data from the Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS) for March 2019, 2020, and 2021, the research uses a quantitative approach to explore how various socioeconomic factors like income, education, occupation, household size, and gender impact spending choices. The results show that income and household size were the main drivers of food and health spending, while education played a significant role in shaping leisure spending in urban areas after the pandemic. The crisis pushed people to prioritize essential goods and digital services. Urban households bounced back more quickly in terms of leisure spending, whereas rural households tended to be more cautious. These differences highlight the vulnerabilities faced by rural and low-income groups, emphasizing the need for targeted policy measures. This research adds to economic theory by applying Engel's Law and Keynesian consumption theory to data from the pandemic era, and it offers policy suggestions aimed at fostering equitable recovery through investments in healthcare, digital infrastructure, and income support.

title: Money, Currency and Contracts: An Alternative view of RTI Ltd v MUR Shipping BV
affiliations: King's College London

detail.title: Money, Currency and Contracts: An Alternative view of RTI Ltd v MUR Shipping BV
detail.abstract: Money and payment are at the epicentre of commercial and financial transactions. Despite this, the legal understanding of both money and payment is elusive. A most recent manifestation of this is the case of RTI Ltd v MUR Shipping Ltd BV where the issue turned on whether a reasonable endeavours proviso required the acceptance of ‘payment in euros’ when the contract stipulated that freight is to be paid in US dollars. The courts referred to this as ‘non-contractual performance’, reducing the primary issue to one of contractual construction. This article disagrees and takes the position that the courts were wrong in viewing what was, in fact, tender of euros - and not payment – as non-contractual performance. Two fundamentally flawed premises are identified: (i) that the offer to pay in euros would have constituted the relevant payment for the discharge of the obligation; and (ii) that acceptance of the offer to transfer euros and cover the conversion exchange fees would have altered the substantive obligation of the contract and would, thus, amount to non-contractual performance. At its core, the cause of this incorrect conception of the relevant monetary obligation was a misunderstanding of the distinction between money of account and money of payment.

detail.title: Large Portfolios under Short-Sale Constraints: Optimality, Estimation Accuracy, and Beating 1/N
detail.abstract: We show that the optimal portfolio under no-short-sale restriction coincides with an unconstrained solution on a subset of assets, and, its Sharpe ratio converges to that of the true optimal portfolio in the special case of a factor model, even though the latter may involve short positions. This implies that long-only investors can potentially approximate efficiency. In high dimensional estimation, the no-short-sale restriction ensures that the estimated optimal portfolio converges to its population counterpart, whereas the unconstrained estimator fails to converge. Perhaps surprisingly, the short-sale constrained portfolio can also outperform the 1/N rule in general.

title: The Optimal and Cost-effective Artificial Lift System (ALS) Combination, Success Case Studies, and Cost Saving Assessment for RRP (Reciprocating Rod Pump) wells in Oman

detail.title: The Optimal and Cost-effective Artificial Lift System (ALS) Combination, Success Case Studies, and Cost Saving Assessment for RRP (Reciprocating Rod Pump) wells in Oman
detail.abstract: With continuous instability of oil prices, it became necessary to reduce the cost of lifting the crude oil from the wells. This cost reduction is not feasible for each stage of the total oil production system; therefore, the optimization of each component in the production system is a must. The primary challenge is to extend the lifting equipment run life, especially the downhole components. For years, operators have been looking for reliable, flexible, and intelligent lifting systems to improve their operating costs, reservoir recovery factor by maximizing well production. Production optimization meant to apply an optimum analysis and comprehensive investigation of well production system; including the artificial lift system that expected to increase the oil production and reduce the operating costs. When producing difficult fluids from marginal, mature, and brown onshore oil fields, Sucker rod (Beam and Progressive Cavity) Pumping systems are typically the most common artificial lift methods used. The primary challenge is to extend the lifting equipment run life, especially the downhole components. Production optimization found to be an essential for the life cycle of each system to extend run life, decrease cost, and increase the cumulative production per well. High WC (90% & above), corrosive environment, sand production & scale build up resulted from water flooding effect are factors that result in harsh operating condition that dramatically affect downhole equipment lifetime & lead to premature failure. In some of the fields premature failures resulted from harsh operating conditions are found close to 70% of total premature failure & 35% of total failures. The failures and problems related to Beam pumping (BP) and the success resulted from the applications of the system optimization has encouraged us to be selected to be the subject of this paper. This presentation will discuss in full details the current downhole pump failures, challenges & plan of improving downhole pump metallurgy, configuration the application using latest technology in BP system. It will share different case histories and best practices from BP Wells by using actual well data and performance. This topic can be summarized in:-• Heavy oil harsh well condition challenges & operational performance of beam pumping system in such these conditions. • Solids & abrasives related failures investigation & solution planning • Success stories maximizing pump efficiencies and minimizing failure rates of beam pumping system • Cost saving impact after using solutions.

title: Can Intellectual property protection policy promote entrepreneurship:evidence from China
affiliations: South China University of Technology, Guizhou Minzu University and South China University of Technology

detail.title: Can Intellectual property protection policy promote entrepreneurship:evidence from China
detail.abstract: AbstractPurpose —This study aims to assess the influence of China’s pilot policy of Intellectual Property Demonstration City (IPDC) on urban entrepreneurial activity. It investigates how the policy influences entrepreneurship through knowledge spillover behaviors and explores the heterogeneous policy effects across regions and industries, providing insights into how intellectual property (IP) protection promotes innovation-driven growth in emerging economies.Design/methodology/approach —The research utilizes the IPDC pilot policy as a quasi-natural experiment and adopts a multi-period difference-in-differences (DID) model to examine panel data from 236 Chinese cities spanning the years 2003 to 2021. Propensity Score Matching (PSM) is used to do the potential self-selection bias. Mechanism and heterogeneity analyses, as well as placebo and robustness tests, are conducted to validate the results.Findings —These indicate the pilot policy of IPDC significantly boosts urban entrepreneurship. The further analysis shows that the effects of the policy are more pronounced in eastern parts, cities at lower administrative tiers and service industry. Mechanism analysis suggests that the policy promotes entrepreneurship by increasing legal knowledge spillovers while reducing illegal ones. Additionally, the study identifies an inverted U-shaped relationship between efforts to curb illegal knowledge spillovers and entrepreneurial activity, suggesting that moderate—rather than excessive—intellectual property(IP) protection is more effective in fostering entrepreneurship.Originality/value —This research offers an in-depth analysis of how IP protection policies influence entrepreneurial activity in developing economies. By focusing on China as a developing economy, it provides meaningful guidance for policy makers on how to design and implement IP policies that foster innovation and entrepreneurship.

title: Silos of Science: Organizational Structure and the Acquisition of Innovation

detail.title: Silos of Science: Organizational Structure and the Acquisition of Innovation

detail.abstract: The search for innovation constitutes a major imperative in public and private settings alike, particularly in large multi-divisional (M-form) organizations including federal agencies and conglomerates. However, the impact of the organizational structure on the search for innovation is less understood. In the public context, studies of the federal research subsidies often logically focus on applicant characteristics and outcomes. Here we examine how the M-form structure affects project evaluation. As our setting, we use the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program administered by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). We show that the agency acts like a firm in the feasibility stage but not at implementation. Moreover, we use patent data and Technology Readiness Levels to describe how the divisions conduct distinct sensemaking processes; the only division seeking radical innovation instead of incremental innovation receives fewer resources. We demonstrate select consequences of M-form decentralization and the decision-making challenges that inhibit the acquisition of innovation by large companies and the public sector alike, shedding light on why small, new firms are well suited to catalyze change.

detail.title: Are People Maximizing an Incomplete Preference? *
detail.abstract: We study how to test whether choices are compatible with maximizing an incomplete preference when we cannot choose the menus from which to observe choices, both theoretically and empirically. Theoretically, we contrast the testable restrictions of the complete and incomplete preference maximization models, showing that once we drop completeness, testing for compatibility becomes computationally hard and may even require an infinite dataset. Empirically, we propose a toolkit to test for compatibility with maximizing an incomplete preference, addressing cases where the analyst might only observe some of the choices a person would make from a menu. We apply this toolkit to compare the performance of the complete and incomplete preference maximization models in three existing choice experiments.
